subject: owlLibrarian
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: great horned owl librarian with spectacles.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I want something unexpected for this owl librarian with spectacles — rather than a typical feather rendering, I'm picturing it built from marbled endpaper textures with gilt book-tooling details, fitting its scholarly, bookish nature.

For the pose and build, I'm thinking humanoid with two arms and legs, standing upright in an A-pose with feathered wing-arms draped like sleeves, perhaps holding a small book, keeping the design manageable while still reading clearly as owl-librarian.

Accessories should stay minimal but meaningful: spectacles with a chain, a gilt-tooled waistcoat, maybe a bow-tie or cravat, and a key or watch chain detail — skipping anything like loose props that aren't explicitly named, so I'll settle on just the glasses, waistcoat, and perhaps a small ribbon bookmark trailing from a tucked book, keeping focus on the ear tufts as the owl's signature feature.

For the marbled paper texture, I'm writing a paint function that uses domain-warped noise to create swirling multi-color veins with combed ink lines, defining a marble helper that takes colors, size, and seed to generate the pattern procedurally.

Then I'm adding directional lighting (warm above, cool below) by shading based on normal direction, using noise and paint utilities exported from the builder SDK, and planning gilt tooling with gold line ornaments on dark leather waistcoat panels.

Now I'm listing the texture set I need: an owl eye decal with yellow iris and gilt ring, a facial disc rim with dark brown border, a barred feather card texture for the chest and ear tufts, a gilt art nouveau fleuron border for the waistcoat front, and book cover tooling for the chatelaine's book prop.

I'm rounding out the texture list with an "EX LIBRIS" pocket label, a flight feather bar pattern, a brass "HEAD LIBRARIAN" name badge, and a gilt cuff trim stripe, settling on roughly eight textures total. Now I'm working out proportions for the great horned owl librarian figure, sketching a stylized humanoid around 1.6 meters tall with a plump body, oversized head, and short feathered legs styled like pantaloons.

I'm defining the leg and foot structure with zygodactyl talons adapted to three-front-one-back for a humanoid stance, and laying out the vertical measurements: ear tufts near the top, head center around 1.4m, hips at 0.74-0.76m, knees around 0.4m, and feet near the floor. From there I start building the skeleton rig, placing the hip joint as the root and running the spine chain upward toward the chest.

Now I'm sketching the spine curve through several control points up to the neck and head, deciding to keep the neck short since owls have hidden necks, and planning separate joints for the head, jaw, and a small hooked beak with upper and lower parts.

I'm working out how to loft the body along the spine chain using a sweep function with a radius profile, extending the start point lower to properly cover the hips.

I'm working out the shift offset so the belly bulges toward the front along the tube's normal frame, leaning toward something like [0,-0.04] despite the uncertainty. For plumage I'm planning marbled paper feather textures—cream with brown barring on the breast, dark mottled on the back—plus a slightly larger waistcoat sweep layered over the torso.

Rather than using sectors (which would just recolor at the same radius), I'm building the waistcoat as its own sweep with a slightly larger radius spanning roughly t=0.12 to 0.8, painted so the front panel reads differently from the back lining, with 180 degrees marking the belly/front side on this vertical tube.

The front panel gets a deep forest-green marbled texture with a gilt border, and I'm carving a V-shaped opening using a position condition so the chest feathers peek through at center front, giving the illusion of an open waistcoat over the owl's plumage. I'm also planning small brass button discs placed along the center-front seam using surface ray hits to position them precisely.

Now I'm figuring out the gilt piping trim along the V edges using a drape path pulled toward nearby surface points, roughly tracing from the collar down to the waist point. Next I'm shifting focus to the owl's head design: a great horned owl with broad facial discs, dark rims, yellow eyes, a small hooked beak, and a white throat patch.

I'm working out the head geometry using a flattened part-sphere scaled wider than tall, positioned above the body, with the ear tufts rising outward from the top corners, and defining a head joint with its own local coordinate orientation so I can place facial features consistently relative to forward/up/right directions.

Sticking with explicit model-space coordinates since the head isn't posed, which keeps orientation simple. For the head parts I'm planning a low-poly flat-shaded sphere for the skull with a slight flattening scale, plus flattened disc shapes for the facial discs on the front.

For the discs, I'm positioning scaled-flat spheres symmetrically on the skull's front surface, then painting them with a radial distance function from the disc center to create concentric ring patterns—darker rim near the edge, lighter tawny tones toward the center, mimicking feather disc coloring.

For eyes, I'm considering decaling an eye texture directly onto each disc surface versus using small separate spheres, leaning toward decal projection since the disc geometry already gives a natural curved surface to wrap the eye drawing onto.

Now moving to the beak: small and hooked, positioned between the discs, built as a tapering swept shape with the upper beak curving down into a hook at the tip, using radius profiles that narrow toward the point.

I'm settling on a dark charcoal-blue color for the beak, closer to a real owl's dark grey-black tone. The lower beak forms a smaller sweep near the jaw joint, rigged to a jaw bone so it can open, and next I'm adding a flattened white throat bib patch beneath the beak.

I'm also sketching in a bow tie/cravat below the neck made from two triangular extrusions plus a knot box, colored oxblood with gilt dots, and planning the ear tufts as layered feather-blade extrusions angled outward from the top of the head.

Working out the orientation math so the blades face forward rather than edge-on — I'm computing the cross product of the pose axes to confirm the thickness direction is roughly horizontal, then adjusting so each blade is a flat plane facing front.

I'll give each tuft three blades per side with varying lengths for a more natural, uneven look.

For the plumage I'm designing a marbled feather paint with a dark center stripe and cream bar, plus a pale shaft line, and making the horn tips solid black. I also want to add angled dark brows above each eye and a thin dark feather rim swept around each facial disc using a closed catmull-rom curve.

I'm positioning the rim ring at the equator of each disc sphere, matching the disc's center and scale so it sits naturally embedded at the widest point, and I'm noting that real owl facial discs typically meet above the beak in a V shape, which I want to replicate.

Now I'm working through the spectacles design — gold-wire circular frames around each eye, with lenses that need to look like glass without hiding the eyes beneath, so I'm considering a pale blue-tinted translucent disc material and running into the limitation that alpha-tested textures can't do true semi-transparency.

I'm resolving this by making the lens texture mostly invisible except for a couple of white diagonal reflection glints and a thin rim highlight, so it reads as glass while the eyes stay visible through it. Then I'm figuring out the full frame structure: the circular rims, a bridge arc over the beak connecting them, and temple arms sweeping back along the sides of the head toward where owl ears would be, positioning everything relative to the head's width and the lens centers.

Working out the exact coordinates now, I'm placing the disc/eye surfaces, extending the spectacle rim slightly in front of the face, and routing the temple arms from the rim out to the sides of the skull, checking whether they clip through the head geometry given the skull's scale and center position.

Checking that the arm point sits near the disc edge, which is acceptable as a slight touch. Now I'm working out the bridge over the beak—a small arc connecting the glasses rims at each side, curving up slightly in the middle—and considering how high the beak shape should extend.

The beak starts near the disc center and tapers toward its tip, sitting lower than the bridge so it passes beneath the spectacles comfortably between the lenses. I'm adjusting the beak's half-width to 0.035 and the rim geometry so the inner edges meet the beak sides cleanly, then aligning the lens vertical center with the eye level.

With the eye decals sized to fit inside the lens radius, I'm moving on to planning the body: treating the wings as arms in an A-pose, working out shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates so the upper arm and forearm lengths stay consistent at roughly 0.25 units each while angling outward about 30 degrees from vertical.

For the limb chains, I'm settling on using three named joints per arm (shoulder, elbow, wrist) with the path naturally extending to a tip joint at the end, matching the same pattern I'll use for legs (hip, knee, ankle) so each limb gets its extra endpoint automatically.

For the owl identity, I'll add hanging flight feathers along the underside of each forearm from elbow to wrist—seven primary feathers, marbled with barring, dangling down and outward like a folded wing, using an extrude array along the arm chain.

Rather than fuss with angle computations for which side faces outward, I'll just interpolate positions directly between shoulder and elbow joints and offset by the outward radius vector—simpler and fully deterministic since the arm geometry is fixed.

For the feather blade orientation, I'm working out the cross product of the thickness and length axes to ensure each feather lies flat facing outward from the arm rather than edge-on, so they're visible as broad shapes from the side.

Now I'm figuring out how to stagger these feathers along the arm so they overlap like shingles, hanging down and layered to form a fringed, feathered-sleeve effect rather than attaching flush along the limb.

I think I'll go with a trailing wing-cloak design instead: a fan of 7 long primary feathers arrayed from the wrist, hanging down and fanning outward at angles roughly -20° to +25° around the vertical axis, facing front-back so they read clearly from the front. This gives a strong silhouette of dark barred feathers hanging beside the body like a drooping wing.

Deciding to keep the hands visible at the front cuff edge, with talon fingers poking out, and place the feather fan plus covert feathers slightly behind the forearm. I'm sketching a helper outline shape for a single feather blade using a tapered point with smoothed edges, designing it so the points trace consistently around the shape for a sharp feather tip.

Working out feather placement along each forearm...

Good, the cross product confirms the plane faces correctly, so I can build a `fanFeather` helper for this. Now I'm figuring out where to mount the fan on the forearm — spacing feather bases from elbow to wrist, offset outward and backward, with the spread angle and feather lengths tuned so the tips land near the wrist.

For the hand, I'm planning a palm capsule extending from the wrist plus four digit chains (thumb, index, middle, ring), each with talons, mirroring an owl-like claw structure. I'll also add a second shorter covert feather row overlapping above the main fan for visual depth, bringing the part count per arm to around 26.

Legs will need hip, knee, ankle joints plus four toes each with two joints, and I'm tallying the total joint budget to stay under 160 across spine, neck, arms, and legs combined. For the finger feathering, I'm sweeping tapered capsules from 0.014 down to 0.01 radius in a marbled tan tone to mimic feathered digits, with darker cone-shaped talons at the tips.

Now I'm working out hand pose geometry: wrist direction, palm orientation facing inward, and spreading the fingers across the z-axis in a fan with the thumb offset forward, computing base and joint positions for each finger relative to the wrist.

For the legs, since owls like great horned owls are feathered all the way down, I'm planning fluffy feathered "trousers" running from hip to knee and continuing fully feathered to the toes, with marbled cream-and-brown barring patterns.

Setting up leg joint positions and IK...

Now I'm working out the toe geometry: three front toes spread at angles with two tapering segments each reaching near ground level, plus a back toe extending behind, and curved talon spikes at the tips that may dip slightly below the floor within the allowed tolerance. I'm setting up a digit helper function to build each toe chain with its name, parent joint, points, radii, color, and talon shape.

For the talons, I'll compute the spike direction numerically by combining the last segment's tangent with a downward bias, and make sure to pass an explicit bone reference for the joint so the spike attaches correctly rather than guessing the nearest joint. Color-wise, I'm planning feathered pale buff toes with dark transverse bars and dark talons at the tips, matching an owl's foot.

For the legs, I'm thickening the thigh feathers like trousers with tapering radius along the leg chain, and adding a gilt garter ring around the knee using a surface loop sweep. I'll skip extra fluff texture and rely on painted barring for the leg feathers, then move on to designing a short fan of five tail feathers behind the hips.

Writing feather blade geometry...

So this gives me a reusable blade helper function taking outline, position, direction, and normal to compute the perpendicular axis automatically. I can apply this same helper to ear tufts, wing feathers, and tail feathers by just varying the normal direction, and the mirroring behavior shouldn't affect the painted pattern orientation.

For chest fluff, I'm scattering feather-textured cards across the breast using a barred cream/brown pattern, around 150 cards flowing downward over the body sweep, but need to make sure they only show through the waistcoat's V-neck opening and don't poke through the fabric.

I'm also adding a ruff of feather cards ringed around the neckline, using a radial arrangement with lean angled outward for a fluffy owl collar effect.

I'm checking that the ruff sits right where the head meets the body, then positioning a bow tie card below it on the chest front, matching the body's curvature at that height.

The waistcoat sits around t≈0.82. Now I'm picking a bookbinder-cloth palette — oxblood, forest green, navy, ochre, cream, gilt, ink, and tawny — to color the waistcoat and coat.

For the owl feather marbling, I want a tawny/brown/cream combed pattern with ink veins, like Spanish marble. I'm writing a marbling function that warps position noise into wavy bands and blends colors using smoothstep transitions.

I'll add a thin third color line where bands cross near zero, plus a second warp octave for complexity. Then I'm writing a lighting function that brightens surfaces based on their normal's y-component, giving a subtle warm-top/cool-bottom tint across the Rgb color arrays.

Now I'm planning the owl's marble color scheme: barred brown-tawny for the back, cream-tawny barring for the breast, green marble with gilt veins for the waist, oxblood marble with ochre combs for the cardigan and sleeves, and matching barred legs, plus decorative page-edge gilding on the book.

For glow effects, I'm reserving that for the amber owl eyes rather than the gilt accents, and considering adding a chatelaine at the hip with hanging keys, scissors, and a small book.

I'm working out the belt placement too, thinking a leather strap swept around the waist loop with a buckle, positioned over the waistcoat using the spine joint's surface loop.

Now I'm figuring out the waistcoat's vertical extent along the spine path, cropping the sweep between roughly y=0.79 and y=1.15 to define the hem line near the hip.

Thinking about the hem placement more, I realize the open bottom would reveal body feathers as a belly bulge below the hip line, giving a "pantaloons" look that's actually fine for the owl. I'll try extending the waistcoat sweep from 0.04 to 0.86 with flat caps at the ends, though a flat disc at the bottom might look too dark and need rethinking.

Deciding caps as none should work fine since the body's inner shape sits just beneath and won't show through from outside views. I'll set the waistcoat radius as the body radius plus 0.014 using the same offset function, then move to designing the arm sleeves with a shoulder joint sphere in marbled oxblood positioned where the arm meets the body at roughly y=1.08, x=±0.23, checking that the radii overlap properly without gaps.

For the palette, I'm settling on green waistcoat, oxblood sleeves, cream/tawny feathers, and gilt accents — a classic bookbinder look, with a navy bow tie dotted in gilt and a dark leather belt with a gilt buckle. I also want to add ochre elbow patches as flattened ellipse decals on the cardigan sleeves, positioning them on the outer-back side of the elbow relative to the arm's downward-outward tilt.

Rather than reasoning through tube orientation angles directly, I'll just cast a ray from behind the elbow toward the sleeve surface to find the correct hit point and normal, then stick the patch geometry there using the sweep's surface.

For the gilt cuff ring, I'm defining a loop on the sleeve surface slightly before the wrist cap (around 92% along the arm), using the arm direction to orient the loop plane correctly.

For head detail, I'm adding scattered feather cards on the crown with marbled brown and white speckled paint, plus cream rictal bristles around the beak base, a dark rim ring around the discs, and angled cream brow extrudes between the eyes to mimic a great horned owl's eyebrow markings.

Now I'm planning the waistcoat details: a brass name plate decal reading "HEAD LIBRARIAN" pinned to the left chest, plus a gilt-stitched pocket design with a pocket watch chain. I'm also listing out the texture set needed, including mirrored eye decals, lens glints, and barred and tan feather card textures for the ruff and chest fluff.

Then I'm adding a tooled book cover texture for the chatelaine book, and deciding against separate waist trim or bowtie patterns in favor of simpler painted detail. For a finishing touch, I want a large gilt owl-in-circle emblem decal on the back of the waistcoat, like an ex libris bookplate.

With around eight textures settled, I'm ready to start writing the actual code, pulling in the necessary imports from the SDK module and the glow kit before building out the roughly 800 lines carefully.

I'll keep the color type local for safety and set up small vector helpers, then start constructing the builder with its named joints, beginning with the hips as the root spine joint.

Building the spine chain next...

Now I'm adding the neck and head joints, pulling the last spine joint from the chain array to anchor them.

Working out the jaw joint position and parentage under the head, then checking the skull's vertical proportions—head center at y=1.44, making sure the skull top plus tuft doesn't make the owl too tall overall.

Comparing to real-world scale (owl ~0.55m, humanoid librarian ~1.5-1.7m), I'm shrinking the leg lengths to bring total height down to roughly 1.65-1.68m. I'm recalculating hip, knee, and ankle heights and reworking the spine path coordinates to match this shorter build.

Now I'm computing the body silhouette radii along the spine and solving the leg geometry -- finding thigh and calf lengths and using distance formulas to position the hip, knee, and ankle joints so the legs reach their target foot placement.

I'm placing the neck and head joints, sizing the skull so it slightly overlaps the body's top cap, and adding a neck ruff for visual continuity. Then I'm working out the arm joint chain -- shoulder, elbow, wrist positions and segment lengths -- and starting to position the wing fan extending down from the wrist.

Checking that the dangling wing fan, legs, and feet don't collide given their x-spacing, then verifying the shoulder joint sits right at the body's surface radius at that height so the joint sphere covers the seam cleanly.

Shoulder-to-body width ratio checks out nicely — big head, cute owl proportions. Now I'm setting up the module metadata and style header, defining the marbled-collage palette constants, and starting a shading helper that computes a brightness factor based on surface normal direction.

Writing marble paint function...

I need to type mix's return as a readonly RGB tuple so shade accepts it, and I'm thinking about using different direction vectors for bars versus speckled noise to avoid overly uniform patterns—horizontal bars for owl breast feathers, subtle paper-grain noise modulation elsewhere.

Now I'm writing the facial disc paint function, which computes radial distance and angle from the disc center, mixes tawny and cream colors based on ring patterns plus noise, darkens toward the rim, and adds subtle radial streak variation—confirming it receives model-space coordinates correctly since it operates on a scaled sphere.

I'm bumping up paint resolution to 2048 for finer texel density given how many small painted parts exist. For the feather blade paint, I'm sketching bar stripes along the length axis using a sine period, marking the shaft with a thin light line down the center, darkening the tip past a length threshold, and layering noise-based marbling throughout.

I'm defining a helper that generates feather outline points as width-scaled coordinates along the length, tapering to a sharp tip, and typing it as a union of plain [x,y] tuples and sharp-tagged tuples to avoid relying on an uncertain import of OutlinePoint.

Writing the blade function next, computing orthogonal axes from the direction and normal vectors, then calling the extrude builder with the feather outline, thickness taper, bevel, and smoothing set to 1 since the tip and base points are far enough apart to avoid corner-cutting conflicts.

Still defining ear tuft geometry...

I'm thinking through the cut-paper collage aesthetic for the extrude walls, wanting them to show a cream "paper core" edge where the surface normal is nearly perpendicular to the plate, which would mimic the look of torn paper edges in real collage work.

To avoid over-complicating things, I'm limiting this paper-core treatment to certain blades (wings, tufts, tail) based on whether their normal is aligned with z or y, rather than applying it everywhere, and I'm also considering other decorative touches like the horn tuft coloring and gilt trim on the body.

Now I'm sketching out the spectacles: two circular lens rims made from swept ring curves positioned symmetrically on either side of the head, plus a small glinting plane for each lens to catch the light.

Checking hinge placement and temple curves against the skull geometry, then working out the chain — since a loop around the neck would be hidden by the ruff, I'm routing the chain from the temple ends down the sides of the head and considering a hanging retainer cord down the chest instead.

Actually, I like the idea of a magnifying glass pendant where the two cords meet — a nice librarian detail with a lens loop and handle. I'll simplify by having the cord attach at the neck ruff rather than the temples, draping it across the waistcoat surface.

For the pendant, I'll ray-hit near the chest to place a magnifier ring and handle facing forward, reusing the lens texture for the glint. Now I need to actually write out the full body compilation code, including the spine sweep call for the body itself.

Writing sweep function for body cross-section...

For the waistcoat, I'm defining a V-shaped opening based on normal direction and position that reveals cream breast fluff, with marbled fabric elsewhere, tuning the V's width and tip height for a clean collage look. I'm also setting the sweep path crop and radius for the waistcoat body along the spine, using flat caps.

Now I'm building the arm chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, parented to the chest joint, and sweeping a tapered sleeve shape over it with a round cap at the shoulder and a flat cap at the cuff where fingers emerge, then painting the sleeve in an oxblood marble pattern along its length.

For the cuff, I'm adding a gilt ring loop near the wrist end of the sleeve and considering whether to add a feathered pale wrist stub extending past the cuff before the hand itself begins.

Now I'm setting up the palm as a flattened feathered sphere near the wrist tip, bone to the arm's end joint, then defining a helper function to build individual fingers with their own bones, points, radius, and color.

Still writing finger helper...

Still plotting finger and toe geometry...

I'm checking that the leg's round cap bottom and foot pad align properly, and confirming the toe sweeps sit correctly on their chain. For floor contact, I'm verifying the toe and talon tips land near y=0, computing talon direction as tangent blended with a downward vector so each spike angles forward and down to touch the ground.

Now I'm setting up leg coloring with marble patterning barred along the length, then placing a gilt knee garter ring—deciding to position it along the thigh at 0.85 toward the knee rather than exactly at the joint, since that region bends smoothly and the garter needs a clean perpendicular cut.

Writing leg sweep code...

I'm scattering feather-textured cards along each leg to create fluffy pantaloon puffs—around 40 per leg, flowing downward and flattened onto the surface, pulling color from the same feather texture used elsewhere, then starting to define the SVG feather texture itself.

Still writing SVG code...

I'm verifying the orientation matches so the root sits at the bottom of the frame and the tip at top, then checking stroke width will render at least 3px when rasterized at 128px. Now I'm figuring out how to scatter chest fluff cards onto the waistcoat V-region using a filter that checks surface normal and position.

Checking the neck ruff spacing and count so cards don't spill into the waistcoat trim, restricting placement to the inner cream area. I'm writing the ring generator for the feather ruff around the neck, setting count, radius, lean, and flow, then confirming ring items without an explicit bone assignment fall back to the nearest joint.

I'll assign the ring's bone to the neck joint so all ruff cards stay rigid together, and with lean 55° tilted toward the downward flow, the cards should droop outward like a real ruff. Checking if a second higher ring is needed, I'm now working out whether the first ring at that radius and height actually clears the skull's lower ellipsoid boundary without the cards sinking into the head geometry.

Now I'm planning three concentric rings of varying radius and count, plus separate scattered cards across the skull crown for a feathered cap effect, and considering adding a fringe ring of small cards around each disc rim for extra texture.

I'll keep the beak charcoal-colored and skip detailing the inner mouth. For the bow tie, I'm placing it at the chest beneath the neck ruff, building a central knot box with two triangular wing extrusions on either side.

The wings get a navy marbled finish with gilded dot accents, positioned and oriented to face forward with a slight downward tilt. I'm adding three brass buttons spaced vertically down the waistcoat center and gilt piping tracing the V-shaped edges of the drape.

Still placing decals...

Now I'm figuring out the belt loop position at the waist bulge, making sure the buckle sits at the front and the loop geometry stays within the body's surface region.

For the buckle, I'm raycasting onto the waist surface to find the hit point, then extruding a small gilt rectangular frame with an inner bar at that location for the buckle shape. Then I'm adding a chatelaine at the hip—raycasting to find the attachment point, placing a small hook sphere, and setting up hanging chains using curve interpolation from the hook downward.

I'm working out how to attach hanging items like a key ring, key, and book to the chain using curve-based sweeps, and thinking through bone assignment for the hips area. For the book, I'm realizing a plain box geometry would wrap the cover texture around all six faces including the spine and page edges, which isn't right—I need a different approach so the texture only shows on the front cover.

Instead I'm building the book from separate parts: back and front cover boards, a cream page block inset between them, and a front cover decal plane positioned slightly in front to carry the actual cover artwork, all sized proportionally and positioned relative to the hook point so the book hangs facing forward.

Now I'm checking placement against the body geometry -- the book sits near the hip at x=-0.21, and I need to verify it clears the thigh and arm radius at that height so it doesn't intersect the leg or sleeve when hanging.

For the keys, I'm planning a small ring with three attached keys, each built from a bow circle, a shaft, and teeth outline extruded into a simple key silhouette.

Still working on keys...

I'm trimming scope to keep the part count manageable, dropping scissors and limiting to two keys on the ring, and now I'm figuring out how to sweep a flat ribbon for the bookmark dangling from the book.

Now I'm working out the eye decal placement with mirroring logic so the angry inner lid slope reads correctly on both sides of the face.

Still designing the eye SVG...

Actually, a simpler and more robust approach is to use a clip-path shaped like the eye, then draw the lid as a filled polygon with a curved top edge inside that clip region, adding a stroke along the curve for the lid line. I'll skip extra details like sclera rim and just keep the iris filled with a black outline plus a pupil.

For lens glints, I'm adding two small white curved highlights in the upper-left of the lens plus a tiny dot, tinted pale blue rather than pure white. For the brass name badge, I'm sketching a rounded gold-gradient plate with an ink border, laying out "HEAD LIBRARIAN" as two stacked lines of bold serif text sized to fit.

Now I'm designing the pocket detail: a pentagon welt outline with dashed gilt stitching and tiny ivy leaf motifs, using an opaque dark forest-green lining fill so the pocket reads clearly against the jacket. For the emblem, I'm setting up a double gilt ring with a simple owl silhouette inside, built from basic ellipse shapes for the body and head.

Still writing owl emblem shapes...

For the book cover, I'm designing a navy background with a gilt double border, corner fleurons, and a central quatrefoil motif with "VOL. I" text. That brings the total count to eight SVGs: eye, lens, cream feather, dark feather, badge, pocket, emblem, and cover.

Now I'm working out the beak geometry with a bezier curve from base to tip, positioning it so the beak protrudes slightly forward of the lens plane by about three centimeters.

Checking that the spectacle bridge rests naturally on the beak base near the owl's nose — the bridge height lines up just above the beak's top edge, so the glasses look perched correctly. I'm also defining a radius taper function for the beak and assigning the beak color to the upper sector.

Now I'm sketching the lower beak curve, placing joint points so the lower tip sits slightly behind and below the upper beak tip, adjusting coordinates by eye to get a believable overlap.

Then I'm checking the beak thickness where it meets the jaw, confirming the radii line up so the beak base appears to fuse smoothly into the skull with no gap.

For the throat, I'm considering adding a small cream-colored sphere beneath the beak to form a bib shape, positioning and scaling it to sit against the skull's underside.

Then I'm placing circular frame rings around each eye disc, approximating the right radius so the ring doesn't clip the eye center, and aligning the disc centers with the eye height.

Now I'm working out the orientation of cards placed around the rim: each should face outward radially from the ring circle, with a slight forward lean to tilt them toward the viewer, so I'm reasoning about how the facing axis and flow direction interact for radial ring items.

I'm checking that rim cards leaning forward at the chosen angle stay within the skull bounds, and planning how to split the left and right rings so their arcs don't overlap at the beak's center — I'll trim the angular range on each ring to avoid doubling up where they meet.

I'll simplify and just use full rings for the brow coverage rather than fussing over exact angle ranges—the slight overlap near the beak is fine and actually mimics real owl whisker tufts. Now moving to the tail: five fanning feather blades rooted near the hips, angled outward in the xz-plane from a base point behind the body.

I'm positioning the tail feathers so they emerge below the waistcoat hem, dipping down and back to create a believable silhouette peeking out from behind the belly dome, then noting remaining small details like the gilt trim and glasses cord still to place.

Now I'm starting the actual code for the "Marbled Endpaper Bindery" style, setting up the imports from the builder library and defining the color palette constants for the piece.

Defining marble paint textures...

Still defining more marble materials...

Still refining the shader logic...

Still working out wing feather placement...

Starting to write the full build function with bone joints and feather geometry...

Still defining joints...

Defining the waistcoat paint logic...

Now I'm setting up the arm chains for both left and right sides, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints symmetrically and parenting them to the chest, plus adding shoulder pad spheres.

Placing an ochre elbow patch using a flattened cylinder oriented along the arm, then starting to sketch cuff loop geometry via a surface-based approach.

Adding cuff loop sweeps...

Now I'm working out the wrist joint for the palm and finger placement, using the last joint in the arm's chain as the wrist anchor and offsetting the palm sphere along the forearm direction. Then I'm setting up the leg geometry with hip and ankle points fed into the limb function to generate bent leg paths for each side.

Writing leg chain setup...

Still writing card and decal setup...

Adding the lens plane with glint and texture, then rim sweeps, hinge blocks, and a draped cord for a hanging magnifier pendant, estimating the waist surface position where it should attach.

Working out the cord's catmull path from the shoulders down to the V-neck center, plotting rough coordinates for each point along the curve.
